messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
Hi,

I am exploring the possibility of simultaneous fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan and combined the code from sections 16.3 and 16.4 of stan user's guide.  The combined code is attached.  I wonder if there are any possibilities to improve the code in order to get predictive posterior distribution faster (such as Cholesky Factorization).  Perhaps I am not able to use the analytical form outlined in 16.4 because eventually I will use informative priors for sigma_sq.

Can you share any insights into this?

Thanks,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
You can certainly Cholesky factor. Then you have to do
your own transform, but I thought there was an example of that in
the manual.

You should probably also look about doing anything predictive in
the generated quantities block. There’s a multi_normal_rng, but not
yet a multi_normal_prec_rng or multi_normal_cholesky_rng.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
You certainly can do that, but it's not going to give
you a different answer than doing it within Stan (unless there's
a bug on one side or the other). Stan's extract function lets
you pull out the parameters for each draw in the sample.

I'm guessing from your traceplot, which shows a huge increase
in variance after adaptation, that what's happened is that the
last step of adaptation found a smaller step size and was thus
able to explore more of the posterior. That is, the post-warmup
draws showing higher variance may be closer to the posterior
than the warmup iterations. My suggestion would be to run
warmup for more iterations and see what the posterior looks like.

You want to inspect what happened to adaptation in the two chains you're
showing. There's no way the posterior measures of convergence R-hat
and n_eff will look good given that traceplot with two chains of very
different means.

- Bob

won't affect the actual sampling algorithm.

It's always good to have an independent test of code.

The thing I'd be most worried about is the difference in behavior
during adaptation and sampling. It's a sign that adaptation hadn't
fully adapted.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
I'd suggest taking smaller steps in moving from your Stan1.stan
to Stan2.stan model. In particular, starting from Stan1.stan,
I'd suggest replacingn

for (n in 1 : N1) y [n] <- y1 [n];
for (n in 1 : N2) y [N1 + n] <- y2 [n];
y ~ multi_normal (mu, Sigma);

with just

y1 ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);

and verifying that mu and Sigma fit as intended, and then
moving the sampling for y2 to the generated quantities block.

- Bob

Hi Linas/Bob,

This thread has been extremely helpful for me to get up to speed on fitting and predicting GP "in one go". Thanks very much guys!

Based on, FitPredict, I have tried to add multivariate input support and automatic relevance determination (Ch 14.2, 14.3, doc: 2.6.2)

1. As per suggestion in the manual, I have made the following changes:

parameters {
....
  vector<lower=0>[D] rho;
.....
}

model {
....
  matrix [N, N] Sigma;
  for (i in 1 : (N - 1)) {
    for (j in i : N) {
      vector[D] tmp_exp_term;
      tmp_exp_term <- rho .* (x[i] - x[j]);

      Sigma [i, j] <- eta_sq * exp (-dot_self(tmp_exp_term));   
    //    exp (-rho_sq * pow (x [i] - x [j], 2));
      Sigma [j, i] <- Sigma [i, j];
    }
  }
....
....
rho    ~ cauchy (0, 5);
}

I want to ask, from efficiency perspective, are there much better ways to do it without moving to Cholesky/analytical form?

2. Attached is a traceplot of selected paramters i have run, with N = 20, D=3. While the predicted y2 have converged quite well, trace of eta_sq and rho seems to have done less well. Is this something I should worry about?

3. Are there sample code using Cholesky and/or analytical form for doing fitting and predicting together over multivariate inputs?

Thanks,

Andy

Yes, there's a problem in that the rho and eta are going to be highly

factoring it, at which point using the Cholesky factor should
be easy.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
> On May 6, 2015, at 3:53 AM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, May 5, 2015 at 4:43:44 AM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I tried to run it for different iter setting. But, it seems that sd of rho would only get worse if i increase the iter from 2k to 100k.

I think the goal should be to get the right posterior sd,
so I'm not sure what you mean by worse --- is this versus
simulated data?
> I am attaching the code, sample data I ran on, summary of the fit objects and traceplots. Again, the predicted y seems to be stable though.

That happens when there is a range of parameter space that produces
similar outputs --- the predictions will have higher n_eff estimates
and better apparent convergence than their basis in coefficients, etc.

>
> One thing to note: the X1/predictors are highly correlated - output from R cor function:
>
> [,1] [,2] [,3]
> [1,] 1.0000000 0.9813094 0.9459689
> [2,] 0.9813094 1.0000000 0.9763934
> [3,] 0.9459689 0.9763934 1.0000000
>
> Would this be an issue? Or, I need a tighter prior on rho?

This can cause problems in fitting. The general thing to do is simulate
data like what you have and see if you can recover the correct values of
the parameters. Given that you're also trying to do prediction of new
y, that should be a reasonable way to evaluate whether what you're
trying to do will work.

- Bob

That happens when there is a range of parameter space that produces
similar outputs --- the predictions will have higher n_eff estimates
and better apparent convergence than their basis in coefficients, etc.

>

>
>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
> [1,] 1.0000000 0.9813094 0.9459689
> [2,] 0.9813094 1.0000000 0.9763934
> [3,] 0.9459689 0.9763934 1.0000000
>
> Would this be an issue? Or, I need a tighter prior on rho?

This can cause problems in fitting.  The general thing to do is simulate
data like what you have and see if you can recover the correct values of
the parameters.  Given that you're also trying to do prediction of new
y, that should be a reasonable way to evaluate whether what you're
trying to do will work.  

- Bob

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
You didn't mention anything about your data or what prior information you have.

I usually scale x to have mean 0 and std 1. Then as a weakly informative prior I would use
 l ~ t(4,0,1)
where l=1/rho is the lengthscale. This prior is quite flat for l<1 and for l>1 the behavior of the GP does not change much (it's already close to linear), so it's unlikely that larger values are needed, but having the thick tail still provides the possibility that the data overrules the prior.

For eta I would use prior which says that eta_sq is likely to be smaller than the total variance of the data.  I usually scale y to have mean 0 and std 1, and thus I can use prior favoring eta<1. Note that, the total variance of the predicted data is eta_sq+sigma_sq, so you could also define a prior on eta_sq+sigma_sq and prior on ratio eta_sq/sigma_sq which is the proportion of the explained variance.


Aki

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gaussian process fitting and posterior predictive distribution in stan
parts:
functional form:
- my prior expectation is that y should be a linear function with zero intercept of x for  "small values" of x (most of the observations) but is bounded by an unknown asymptote values on both positive and negative ends. The intuition is that y will react to x linearly, but only up to a certain extend. Beyond that, an incremental change would have increasingly small impact on y.

I assume you mean "close to linear" and not "linear". If you assume saturation, you should use some sigmoid function possibly combined with a GP, instead of just GP with a prior mean zero and a stationary covariance function.

Data size:
- number of observations(N): typically, 10 - 15
- number of x(D): can be up to 15

The latest model I found in this thread was t_gp_fp.stan. It has a GP prior with squared exponential covariance function allowing nonlinearities and full interactions. If rho is large for all dimensions, then you have too much flexibility compared to your small N. Since your x's are highly correlated, it would be useful use factor analysis distance (projecting x's to a lower dimensional manifold). Alternatively you need to have a strongly sparsifying prior for rho and hope that only one (or two) dimensions will be used. 

 Aki
